stages.title: Advanced clinical reasoning
stages.hook: A test is positive. Does that make the disease likely? The answer depends on what you believed before the test. How should a result move your belief?
explain: Good reasoning is probabilistic. Start with a pre-test probability from the patient's story, risk factors and local disease frequency. A test result updates it. The likelihood ratio (LR) summarises how much: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. Using odds: post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR, where odds = p ÷ (1 − p).

Clinicians also use thresholds. If probability is below the test threshold, no test is needed; between the test and treatment thresholds, testing is useful; above the treatment threshold, treat. The thresholds are lower when the disease is dangerous and treatment is safe, and higher when treatment is risky.

Reasoning errors arise from heuristics (anchoring, availability, premature closure, base-rate neglect), from system factors (fatigue, interruptions, poor handover) and from information problems. Strategies include a diagnostic time-out, asking what else it could be, a pre-mortem ('if I am wrong, how?'), cognitive forcing, second opinions, and following up uncertain cases with safety-netting (clear advice on what to watch for and when to return).

example.q: Pre-test probability of a disease is 20%. A test has LR+ of 8 and is positive. What is the post-test probability?

analogies.home: A smoke alarm in a kitchen that is frequently smoky means less than one in a quiet bedroom.

stages.title: Multisystem disease assessment
stages.hook: A single infection can affect lungs, kidneys, blood pressure and consciousness. How do clinicians keep track of many organs at once?
explain: Many diseases involve more than one organ system: sepsis, diabetes, vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, heart failure with kidney and liver involvement, and cancer. A multisystem assessment reviews each system systematically, looks for patterns across systems, and asks whether one process explains several findings or whether several processes coexist.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Bedside tools such as qSOFA flag higher risk when two or more are present: respiratory rate of 22 or more per minute, altered mentation, systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less. These are screening aids, not diagnoses; clinical concern always counts. Organ dysfunction can be tracked with scores such as SOFA, which combines breathing, clotting, liver, circulation, brain and kidney measures.

Look for organ-by-organ clues: brain (confusion, Glasgow Coma Scale), lungs (oxygen level, breathing rate), circulation (blood pressure, lactate, capillary refill), kidneys (urine output, creatinine), liver (bilirubin), and blood (platelets). Early recognition, prompt treatment of the cause (for example controlling the source of infection), supporting organs and frequent reassessment improve outcomes. Chronic multisystem disease demands coordinated care by several specialties to avoid conflicting advice.

example.q: A fictional adult with pneumonia has RR 28, new confusion and systolic BP 90 mmHg. What is the qSOFA score and what does it suggest?
steps: Systolic BP ≤ 100: 1 point, so total 3. A score of 2 or more flags high risk of poor outcome; escalate urgently for sepsis management.
example.a: qSOFA 3, high risk; treat as possible sepsis and escalate urgently

stages.title: Critical care and emergency decision-making
stages.hook: In a resuscitation, seconds matter and information is incomplete. How do teams make safe decisions under pressure?
explain: Critical care supports failing organs while the cause is treated. Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. Main types: hypovolaemic (loss of volume, such as bleeding), cardiogenic (pump failure), distributive (widened vessels, as in sepsis or anaphylaxis) and obstructive (blockage, such as a large pulmonary embolism or tension pneumothorax). Treatment targets the type, so identifying it matters.

Respiratory failure may be type 1 (low oxygen) or type 2 (high carbon dioxide). The ratio PaO₂/FiO₂ describes oxygenation: for example, PaO₂ 60 mmHg on 50% oxygen (FiO₂ 0.5) is 120, which is markedly impaired (normal is above about 400). Support can range from oxygen by mask to non-invasive ventilation to mechanical ventilation, which carries risks and requires careful sedation and monitoring.

Decision-making in emergencies uses structured approaches (ABCDE, team roles with a clear leader, closed-loop communication, SBAR), anticipates deterioration, and includes ethical thought: patients' prior wishes, capacity, and treatment-limitation decisions such as do-not-attempt-resuscitation orders, which are made through communication with patient and family in advance where possible. Human factors such as fatigue, hierarchy that stops juniors speaking up, and fixation errors are common causes of harm; speaking up and debriefing improve safety.

example.q: After a road accident a fictional patient has pulse 135, BP 75/40, cold skin and a distended abdomen. Which type of shock and what priority?
steps: Trauma with a fast pulse, low BP and cold skin suggests bleeding.
This is hypovolaemic shock from loss of blood volume.
Priority: call the trauma team, control bleeding, restore circulating volume with blood, and get urgent surgical control.
example.a: Hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock; call the trauma team and control bleeding urgently

stages.title: Clinical pharmacology and treatment evaluation
stages.hook: Two patients take the same medicine. One has too little effect and the other has side effects. Why does the same drug act differently in different people?
explain: Pharmacokinetics (what the body does to the drug) shows that clearance and volume of distribution determine half-life: the time for the drug concentration to fall by half. Steady state with repeated dosing is reached after about 4 to 5 half-lives. After one half-life, 50% remains; after two, 25%; after three, 12.5%. Oral drugs may undergo first-pass metabolism in the liver, reducing the amount reaching the circulation.

Pharmacodynamics (what the drug does to the body) includes receptor binding, efficacy, potency and the dose-response relationship. Differences between people arise from age, weight, kidney and liver function, genetics (pharmacogenomics), other medicines (enzyme inhibition or induction), pregnancy, and adherence. Narrow-therapeutic-index drugs may need blood-level monitoring.

Evaluating treatment asks whether a medicine achieves what matters to patients (clinical outcomes such as fewer strokes rather than only a lab number), at what harm and cost. Surrogate outcomes may mislead. Post-marketing surveillance detects rare harms that trials miss, and clinicians report suspected adverse reactions. Prescribing should follow indication, review and stopping rules; deprescribing is part of good care. This game gives no doses or regimens.

stages.title: Advanced diagnostic interpretation
stages.hook: A blood gas shows pH 7.25, low bicarbonate and fast deep breathing. What story do the numbers tell?
explain: Arterial blood gases are read in steps: Is the pH acidic (below 7.35) or alkaline (above 7.45)? Is the primary change in carbon dioxide (respiratory) or bicarbonate (metabolic)? Is there compensation? Reference values used here: pH 7.35 to 7.45, PaCO₂ 35 to 45 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 to 26 mmol/L. Low pH with low bicarbonate means metabolic acidosis; low pH with high PaCO₂ means respiratory acidosis.

The anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate); a typical range is about 8 to 12 mmol/L (laboratories vary). A raised gap points to added acids, such as lactate or ketones. Lactate rises when tissues lack oxygen. In metabolic acidosis the lungs compensate by breathing faster and deeper to blow off CO₂.

Other interpretation skills: reading the ECG systematically (rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR interval, QRS, ST segments, T waves), noticing ST elevation as a sign of an acute artery blockage, and the chest X-ray (airway, breathing, circulation, diaphragm, everything else). Always combine investigations with the patient: an abnormal result in a well person and a normal result in a very sick one both need careful thought. Request, check, and act on critical results, and document your reasoning.

example.q: pH 7.25, PaCO₂ 25 mmHg, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, Na 138, Cl 100. What is the acid-base pattern and anion gap?
steps: pH is low: acidaemia. Bicarbonate is low, so the primary problem is metabolic acidosis.
PaCO₂ is low: the lungs are compensating by blowing off CO₂.
Anion gap = 138 − (100 + 10) = 28, which is raised; think of lactate or ketones.
example.a: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation and a raised anion gap of 28

stages.title: Public health and epidemiology
stages.hook: A new infection appears. Each case infects two others, then four, then eight. How do public health teams decide what to do, and when can an outbreak stop?
explain: Epidemiology studies how often disease occurs and why. Incidence is the number of new cases in a population at risk over a time period; prevalence is the proportion with the disease at a time. A rate allows fair comparison between populations of different sizes. Descriptive epidemiology uses person, place and time; analytic studies (cohort, case-control, trials) test causes.

The basic reproduction number R₀ is the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. If R₀ > 1 an outbreak grows. The herd immunity threshold is approximately 1 − 1/R₀: with R₀ = 4, about 75% need to be immune. The effective reproduction number R takes account of immunity and control measures; control aims to push R below 1.

Public health acts at three levels: primary prevention (before disease occurs, such as vaccination, clean water, tobacco control), secondary prevention (early detection, such as screening) and tertiary prevention (reducing the impact of established disease, such as rehabilitation). Surveillance, contact tracing, outbreak investigation and clear communication are core tools. Social determinants such as income, education, housing, and access to services strongly shape health, so equity is a key aim. Screening must weigh benefits against false positives and overdiagnosis.

example.q: A disease has R₀ = 5. What proportion of the population needs to be immune for herd immunity (assuming a simple model)?
steps: So about 80% need to be immune.

Ongoing collection and analysis of health data for action.
Conditions in which people live and work that shape health.

misc.wrong: Public health is just about treating sick people.
misc.right: Public health focuses on preventing disease and protecting health across populations, including clean water, vaccination and fair access to care.

R₀ = 2. What percentage must be immune for herd immunity, using 1 − 1/R₀?
If R is below 1...
o: The outbreak declines
The outbreak grows faster
Nothing changes at all
Everyone in the community is infected

o: Secondary prevention
Primary prevention before any disease starts
Tertiary prevention after complications
Treatment of established disease only

o: Tertiary prevention
Primary prevention
Secondary prevention
Screening
questions.why: Tertiary prevention reduces the impact of established disease.

questions.q: Prevalence differs from incidence because it...
o: Counts all existing cases at a time, not only new ones
Counts only the deaths in a year
Counts only new cases in a period
Measures the cost of care to the system

questions.q: A fictional village has a surge of diarrhoea after flooding. What is a first public health step?
o: Ensure safe water and sanitation, and investigate the outbreak
Ignore it until more people are ill
Close all clinics in the district
Stop surveillance to save resources
questions.why: Break the water-borne chain and gather data.

questions.q: Order an outbreak investigation.
items: Confirm the diagnosis and the outbreak
Describe cases by person, place and time
Form and test hypotheses on the cause

questions.q: Explain why social determinants such as housing and income matter for health.
questions.model: Housing, income and education shape exposure to risks and access to care, so inequality produces unfair differences in illness, which is why public health works on these conditions as well as on medical services.

panel.q: A screening test finds many early abnormalities that would never have caused harm. What is the problem?
o: Overdiagnosis, leading to unnecessary worry and treatment
More benefits for everyone screened
No effect on anyone at all
A cure for the cancers found

o: Listen, work with community leaders and give clear honest information
Shame people into attending clinics
Force vaccination on everyone
Remove services from the community

panel.q: Why can R differ between places or times even for the same infection?
panel.model: R depends on how people mix, how many are immune and what control measures are in place, so it changes between places and over time even if the microbe is the same.
panel.why: R is not a fixed property of a microbe.

teach.model: R₀ is how many people one case infects. If it is above 1, the outbreak grows. Vaccines and control measures reduce spread, and the herd immunity threshold is about 1 − 1/R₀. Public health also works on clean water, screening and fair access to care.

What else does public health do?

stages.title: Clinical research and biostatistics
stages.hook: Two studies of the same drug disagree. One finds a benefit, the other finds none. How can both be honest work?
explain: Research questions are framed with PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome. Designs include randomised controlled trials (strongest for treatments), cohort studies (follow groups forward), case-control studies (compare people with and without a disease looking back), cross-sectional surveys and qualitative studies. Phases of drug trials: phase 1 (safety), phase 2 (early efficacy and side effects), phase 3 (large comparison), phase 4 (post-marketing).

Bias is a systematic error (selection, measurement, reporting); chance is random error. Confounding makes an apparent link appear. Sample size and power determine the chance of detecting a true effect. A 95% confidence interval is a range that, across many repeated studies, would contain the true value in about 95% of them; approximate 95% CI = estimate ± 1.96 × standard error. A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if there were truly no effect; p < 0.05 does not prove the effect is real or important, and p > 0.05 does not prove no effect.

Survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier curves, hazard ratios) handles time-to-event data. Multiple testing, subgroup fishing and stopping early inflate false positives. Research ethics requires independent review, informed consent, minimising harm, honest reporting, trial registration, and fair inclusion. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses pool trials, but combine good evidence only if the included trials are sound ('garbage in, garbage out').

example.q: A trial estimates a mean drop of 10 mmHg in blood pressure with standard error 2 mmHg. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval?

analogies.sport: A coin tossed ten times may show seven heads by chance, whereas a thousand tosses give a steadier answer.
analogies.home: Weighing a bag of rice once may be off; averaging many weighings is steadier.
analogies.city: A poll of ten people tells less than a well-chosen sample of thousands.
analogies.tech: A single test run can fail by chance; many runs show the true pattern.

stages.mnemonic: PICO to ask, random to compare, CI to show precision, ethics to protect.
terms: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome: a way to frame a research question.
A range of values consistent with the data, showing precision.
Probability of results at least this extreme if there were truly no effect.
The chance a study detects a real effect of a given size.
Relative rate of an event over time in one group compared with another.

misc.wrong: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 97% chance the treatment works.
misc.right: The p-value is about the data if there were no effect; it does not give the probability that the treatment works.

stages.limits: Frequentist and Bayesian approaches interpret probability differently, and statisticians disagree about the best way to report results.

trip.prompt: Find how the width of a confidence interval changes with sample size.

questions.q: Estimate 5 and standard error 1.5. Using 1.96 × SE, what is the upper limit of the approximate 95% CI, to one decimal place?
In a cohort, 30 of 200 exposed people and 10 of 200 unexposed people develop disease. What is the relative risk?
A 95% CI for a risk ratio is 0.8 to 1.3. What does this suggest?
o: The data are consistent with no effect (1.0 is inside)
Strong benefit from the treatment
Strong harm from the treatment
An impossible result that must be an error
questions.why: A CI including 1 for a ratio means no clear difference.

questions.q: Which design is generally the strongest for testing a treatment?
o: Randomised controlled trial
A single case report from one hospital
Expert opinion alone
A patient anecdote

questions.q: A larger sample size generally leads to...
o: A narrower confidence interval
A wider confidence interval
More bias in the result
No change at all in the interval

questions.q: Match the phase to its main aim.
A study tests 40 subgroups and reports the one with p = 0.03 as a finding. What is the concern?
o: Multiple testing makes chance findings likely
None, since the finding is significant
Subgroups are always valid evidence
p < 0.05 always proves that the treatment works
questions.why: With many tests, some will be falsely significant.

questions.q: Order the stages of a typical clinical trial.
items: Register the protocol and get ethics approval
questions.why: Good practice from question to honest report.

questions.q: A trial stops early after a favourable interim result. What is a concern?
o: It may overestimate the effect
It always underestimates the harms of treatment
It is always better than a full trial
There is no concern at all
questions.why: Early stopping for benefit can exaggerate effect sizes.

questions.q: Explain why p > 0.05 does not prove that a treatment has no effect.
questions.model: A non-significant result may come from a small, underpowered study, so absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; the confidence interval shows which effects are still plausible.

panel.q: A meta-analysis pools twenty small trials, most of poor quality. How reliable is the result?
o: Limited, since pooling poor studies does not remove their bias
Perfect, because the pooling adds many patients
Always correct, as the results are combined
Unaffected by the quality of the trials

panel.q: A trial excludes older people and pregnant women. What is a consequence for guidelines?
o: Results may not apply to those groups
Results apply equally to every group
Nothing changes for the guidelines
Guidelines become perfect for all people

panel.q: Why must trials be registered and all outcomes reported?
panel.model: Registration with pre-specified outcomes and full reporting prevents selective publication of positive results, so evidence reflects all the data and decisions about patients are not distorted.

teach.model: Frame the question with PICO, compare groups fairly with randomisation, and look at the confidence interval to judge precision. A p-value is not the chance that a treatment works. Small or biased studies can mislead, so transparent reporting and ethics matter.

points.ask: How is a research question framed?
How do I read the numbers?

stages.title: Healthcare technology and medical AI
stages.hook: An AI reads chest X-rays as well as a specialist in testing. Does that mean it is ready to be used in every hospital tomorrow?
explain: Healthcare technology includes electronic health records, telemedicine, wearable sensors, medical devices, robotic surgery, laboratory automation, imaging systems and clinical decision-support. Benefits are access, speed, consistency and better information; risks are errors, alert fatigue, workflow disruption, security breaches and inequity of access.

Medical AI, usually machine learning, finds patterns in data, such as signs of disease in images. Performance is described with sensitivity, specificity, AUC and predictive values, which depend on prevalence. A tool must be validated on data that were not used for training, ideally externally in different hospitals and populations and prospectively in real use. Models can fail when data shift (different scanners, patient groups or practices), when training data reflect bias or are unrepresentative, or when they learn shortcuts (for example a hospital label on an image rather than the disease).

Safe use requires human oversight with clear responsibility (the clinician remains accountable), transparency about limitations, monitoring after deployment, privacy and data protection, informed consent for data use where appropriate, and regulation of medical devices and software. Explainability helps trust but does not replace validation. Automation bias, over-reliance on a machine's output, is a real risk, as is under-use where the tool would help. Digital tools can widen inequity if some groups lack access, so design and testing should include diverse users. AI should support, not replace, communication and care.

example.q: An AI tool has 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity for a disease with 1% prevalence. In 10,000 screened people, how many true positives and false positives?
steps: So among 590 positives, only 95 (about 16%) are true: low positive predictive value because the disease is rare.
example.a: 95 true positives and 495 false positives, so most positive flags are false

analogies.home: A smoke detector tuned to detect every fire will also go off at toast.
analogies.tech: A model trained on one camera may fail on another.
analogies.sport: An analyst's tool trained on one league may misjudge another.
analogies.city: Traffic software tuned for one city may fail in another with different roads.

stages.mnemonic: Validate outside, watch for shift, keep a human accountable.
terms: Computer methods that learn patterns from data.
Testing a model on data from different sites that were not used to build it.
A change in the data after deployment that lowers performance.
Providing care at a distance using communication technology.

misc.wrong: If an AI is accurate in a test, it is safe everywhere.
misc.right: Performance may fall with different patients, equipment or prevalence, so local validation, monitoring and human oversight are needed.

Share the records openly with other companies

panel.q: Explain why a model's high accuracy on a test dataset does not guarantee safety in practice.
panel.model: A model may perform differently on new populations, equipment or prevalence, or may have learned shortcuts, so external, prospective validation and ongoing monitoring are needed.

teach.model: Medical AI finds patterns in data, but it can fail on new patients or equipment. It must be tested on independent data, monitored, and used with human oversight. Privacy, fairness and clear responsibility matter.

stages.title: Integrated virtual hospital case-management project
stages.hook: A fictional patient arrives in your emergency department with several problems at once. Can you bring together everything you have learned to keep her safe?
explain: This capstone brings together history, examination, reasoning, investigations, treatment principles, communication and ethics in one fictional case. Case: Mrs A, 72, with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and mild chronic kidney disease, presents with 3 days of cough, fever and increasing breathlessness, and now new confusion. Observations: RR 26, SpO₂ 89% on air, HR 118, BP 92/55, temperature 38.9 °C. She takes several regular medicines. This is a simulation, not advice.

Step by step: (1) Recognise she is seriously unwell: ABCDE, give oxygen as indicated, get IV access and call a senior early. (2) Think: likely pneumonia with sepsis and possible organ dysfunction; also consider heart failure, pulmonary embolism, and diabetic problems; keep dangerous causes on the differential. (3) Investigate: blood tests (count, kidney function and electrolytes, glucose, lactate, cultures before antibiotics where it does not delay treatment), blood gas, ECG, chest X-ray. (4) Treat the cause and support organs promptly, review medicines that may be unsafe with kidney injury, and reassess often.

Alongside, practise good care: explain in plain words, check what matters to her and her family, assess capacity (confusion may affect it), act in her best interests if she lacks capacity, respect confidentiality, document clearly, hand over with SBAR, report any error or near miss, and plan safe discharge or ongoing care with follow-up. Reflect afterwards: what went well, what you were unsure about, and what you will learn next. Acting safely means knowing your limits and asking for help.

example.q: In the case above, which three findings most strongly signal a need for immediate senior escalation?
steps: Low oxygen (SpO₂ 89%) with a fast breathing rate of 26 shows respiratory compromise.
Low blood pressure with a fast pulse and new confusion suggest shock and brain involvement; qSOFA is 3.
Fever with a chest source suggests sepsis. Together these need immediate senior help.
example.a: Respiratory compromise (SpO₂ 89%, RR 26), low BP with fast pulse, and new confusion with fever

analogies.sport: A match is won by teamwork, planning and adapting, not one star play.
analogies.sea: Navigating a ship needs charts, instruments, a crew and a captain willing to change course.
analogies.tech: A complex system needs monitoring, backups and clear communication between teams.
analogies.city: A city emergency response coordinates fire, ambulance, hospitals and communication.

stages.mnemonic: Recognise, Resuscitate, Reason, Result-check, Reassess, Respect, Record, Reflect.
terms: A final project that brings together everything learned.
Calling a more senior clinician for help.
A decision-making standard for patients who lack capacity.
Passing key information to the next team using a clear structure.

misc.wrong: Competent doctors manage the hardest cases alone.
misc.right: Competent doctors know their limits, work in teams and escalate early.

stages.limits: A simulation cannot capture every real-world complexity; actual management follows local guidelines and senior clinicians, and no doses or regimens are given here.

Send her to the waiting room until a bed is free
Book an outpatient scan for next week

Tonsillitis only, with no other cause
Back strain from lifting
Sunburn from the day before

To fill time while waiting for a bed
Kidneys do not matter in an acute illness
Medicines never change in safety during illness

questions.q: Order a sensible approach to Mrs A.
items: Recognise she is critically ill and call for help
Take samples and investigations, then treat the cause promptly
Reassess and communicate with her and family
questions.why: Recognise, stabilise, investigate and treat, reassess.

questions.q: Match the investigation to the question it answers.
pairs: Which germ is in the blood?
How severe is the acid-base and perfusion problem?
Is there a rhythm problem or ischaemia?

questions.q: Mrs A is confused and refuses a procedure. What is the correct first step?
o: Assess her capacity for this decision and act in her best interests if she lacks it
Do the procedure by force
Ignore her wishes and proceed
Ask a stranger in the corridor to decide

questions.q: A nurse notices that a prescribed medicine may be unsafe given her kidney results. What is best?
o: Pause and discuss with the prescriber and pharmacist
Give it anyway as it was prescribed
Hide the chart until the doctor returns
Wait for the next day to raise it

questions.q: Describe how you would hand over Mrs A to the night team using SBAR.
questions.model: Situation: Mrs A, 72, with pneumonia and sepsis. Background: diabetes, hypertension and mild kidney disease. Assessment: low oxygen, fast breathing, low BP and confusion. Recommendation: frequent observations, early senior and critical care review, and reassessment of treatment and kidney function.

panel.q: Mrs A improves, but a junior realises they gave wrong information to the family earlier. What should they do?
o: Correct it honestly, tell the senior and report the error
Say nothing and hope it is forgotten
Blame the family for misunderstanding
Hide the record of what was said

panel.q: The family asks if she is 'going to die'. Her outcome is uncertain. What is the best response?
o: Be honest about the seriousness and uncertainty, show compassion and offer regular updates
Promise that she will definitely be fine
Refuse to speak to the family about it
Give a false certainty to reassure them

panel.q: Reflect: name one thing you would do differently to reduce diagnostic error in a complex case like Mrs A's.
panel.model: I would keep a broad differential, pause for a diagnostic time-out to check for anchoring, and seek senior input so that dangerous alternatives are not missed.

teach.model: In a seriously unwell patient, recognise danger, check ABCDE, call a senior early, think about dangerous causes, investigate and treat the cause, and reassess often. Communicate honestly, respect the patient's choices, hand over clearly and learn from errors.
